citations.evidenceText: Facial task 80 ms, speech 120 ms; independent concurrent processing and ignored fusion delay give max(80,120)=120 ms.

questions.stem: In a supplied ideal motion exercise, a robot moves by perpendicular displacements 300 mm horizontally and 200 mm vertically along one straight segment, returns along that segment, and repeats this round trip 12 times. Assume constant speed equal to 60% of the supplied 8.2 m/s, with instantaneous reversals and no acceleration time. What are total path length and elapsed motion time, rounded only at the end to two decimals?
questions.subtopic: Straight-line round trips and ideal travel time
assumptions: Perpendicular Cartesian displacements; 12 complete out-and-back cycles; fixed ideal speed; no stops, acceleration or deceleration; the supplied speed is not a hardware safety rating.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 57: Week 12 item 4, motion description, given speed, choices and full geometric working
citations.evidenceText: Displacements .300 m and .200 m along one straight line; return; 12 cycles; supplied maximum 8.2 m/s and factor .60; solution uses Euclidean segment length.

solution.justification: Distance is path length, not net displacement, which is zero after complete round trips. The idealized speed and instantaneous reversals are exercise assumptions, not a validated operating command for a physical robot.

optionExplanations.o1: One segment is √(0.3²+0.2²) m; 24 segments total 8.653323... m, divided by 4.92 m/s.
optionExplanations.o2: This counts only 12 outbound segments and omits the returns.
optionExplanations.o3: This adds perpendicular component magnitudes instead of using the straight-line diagonal.
optionExplanations.o4: This uses the full 8.2 m/s instead of the stipulated 60% operating speed.

steps: Convert 300 mm=0.3 m and 200 mm=0.2 m.
Round final outputs: D=8.65 m and t=1.76 s.

assumptions: Orthogonal displacements; n full round trips; v>0 constant; instantaneous reversals; no dwell time.

questions.stem: Which feature in the assignment is a physical yielding mechanism that can take up impact energy without first relying on software to command a stop?
questions.subtopic: Mechanical compliance versus sensing and stopping
assumptions: Compare the physical mechanism, not overall system safety certification; compliance can store and later return energy, so absorption is not assumed to mean irreversible dissipation.

options.text: Mechanical compliance in soft joints or back-drivable actuation.
Emergency-stop decision logic while retaining an otherwise rigid contact path.
Software-defined safety zones while retaining an otherwise rigid contact path.
Redundant sensing while retaining an otherwise rigid contact path.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 59: Week 12 item 10, cobot impact question, four mechanisms and soft-joint explanation
citations.evidenceText: Mechanical compliance is identified; the explanation cites soft joints and back-drivable actuators.

solution.justification: Physical yielding can take up energy through deformation or motion. Compliance need not dissipate all that energy, and it does not by itself establish that a collision is safe.

optionExplanations.o1: Mechanical compliance permits physical yielding, unlike the listed sensing/decision mechanisms alone.
optionExplanations.o2: Additional sensing improves observation but does not itself create a compliant mechanical contact path.
optionExplanations.o3: A software-defined zone can trigger a response but is not itself material or joint compliance.
optionExplanations.o4: Stop logic is a decision/control mechanism, not an elastic or back-drivable yielding element.
